newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's farm minister sees grain output recovery.
newsitem.headline: Russia's farm minister sees grain output recovery.

text.p: Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun said on Wednesday he was still bullish about Russia's harvest prospects, telling the Izvestiya newspaper he saw net grain output at 80 million tonnes.
"This year, we are expecting around 80 million tonnes, nearly 10 million tonnes more than in 1996," he said in an interview with the newspaper.
Ministry officials have already provided official production forecasts of around 80 million tonnes this year. Russia produced 69.3 million tonnes in 1996 and 63.4 million in 1995.
Despite the forecast of recovery, a harvest of 80 million tonnes would still be below the 1991-1995 average crop of about 88 million tonnes.
Khlystun said Russia's 1997 grain imports would be around one million tonnes, mainly for remote regions in the east of the country, while exports would be about the same.
He also repeated his conviction that the farm sector must continue to wean itself from state support.
"They (farmers) understand they can't rely on God or on the government, only on themselves," he said.

The government has encouraged commercial banks to finance an increasing proportion of the country's agricultural industry, as the Soviet system of centralised support and Kremlin-controlled imports is disbanded.
But Khlystun said banks were often reluctant to forward money to farms to finance equipment, fertilisers and fuel, because they viewed the sector as risky.
"Extending credits to the agricultural sector is a complicated and risky procedure," he said.
The need to establish smoother relations between farmers and bankers was especially great now because little money had been set aside for the farm sector in next year's budget.
Khlystun said Russia imported 35 percent of its total food needs each year, a level which has been steady since the mid-1980s.
"If you do not count those foods which we have never produced in this country and will never produce, the share of imports is around 24 percent," he said. "This is a lot."

But he added that the type of foods imported had changed over the last two decades. In the 1980s, Russia bought huge quantities of grain on world markets, but now it imported mostly meat, dairy and other products.
The shift was related to the collapse of the country's livestock sector -- a slump which would be difficult to reverse.
"We need to rejuvenate livestock numbers and the system of securing fodder, but for that we need investment," he said.

Other proposals under consideration by the farm ministry were a federal agency to regulate the food market and a more competitive basis for food purchases by state customers like the army and border guards across Russia's vast terrain.
